opinions.rationale: Inverted search did not find a standard that closes this gap. Feuerriegel et al. (Nat Med 2024) restate that causal ML requires the same identification assumptions as classical methods and does not identify contrasts the data cannot support; that is prior art for the claim, not a solution. Hill and Su (Ann Appl Stat 2013) and Nethery et al. (Ann Appl Stat 2019) give BART-centered common-support diagnostics and nonoverlap-aware estimation, and propensity-score density/trim diagnostics remain routine for low-dimensional scores. Those tools do not constitute a diagnostic in common use that flags, for a general flexible nuisance (including neural nets) and for the same high-dimensional conditioning sets the nuisance uses, which predictions are interpolation versus extrapolation. Package activity in TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, lmtp, WeightIt, and related tools still emphasizes IPW weight extremity and classical overlap plots rather than per-prediction support maps for flexible outcome models. Failure-awareness scoring against deliberately non-identifiable simulations is not an established methods-comparison standard. The problem remains open as stated for applied flexible nuisance work; the caveat is that specialized support diagnostics for some nonparametric models already exist and should be named rather than implied to be nonexistent.

Kim et al. (JAMIA Open 2026; THESEUS) and Wang et al. (npj Digit Med 2026) build or specify automated protocol-to-code and operational EHR mappings; they are the systems whose silent estimand-shift risk the problem names, not fixes of that risk. Lee et al. (JMIR Med Inform 2025) validate LLM-generated trial-criteria queries for functional correctness, which is partial operational testing but not temporal-logic unit tests that distinguish treatment-before versus treatment-after eligibility. Girshovitz, Zeltzer, and Gilad-Bachrach (arXiv:2607.21173, 2026) propose ARA: structured protocol intermediate form, SCM synthetic failure scenarios, and adversarial validation so that silent success is replaced by visible protocol or diagnostic failure. That is closely aligned with the report direction, yet it is a proposal with a small econometric-style benchmark; it does not establish a standard validation regime for TTE automation, dual human sign-off on specification and cohort counts, or synthetic patients that isolate each temporal join. Guidance (TARGET 2025 reporting; FDA/EMA RWE documents) addresses transparency of human-designed emulations, not untrusted machine-generated code. No CRAN or GitHub merge was found that ships a constrained TTE compiler with temporal unit tests. Silent estimand substitution under syntactically valid pipelines remains open.

The report frames embedding adjustment as an open risk without naming the literature that already defines and partially remediates it. Daoud, Jerzak, and Johansson (NAACL 2022) formalize treatment leakage when text is used as a confounder proxy, including leakage from pre-assignment documents that anticipate treatment. Daoud, Johansson, and Jerzak (arXiv:2601.02400, late 2025/2026) add formal definitions, four distillation methods (similarity passage removal, distant-supervision passage classification, salient-feature removal, iterative nullspace projection), and simulation plus empirical sensitivity analysis; they explicitly address the paradox that pre-timestamped text can still encode treatment. That is real prior art for detection and mitigation, not mere restatement. Residual openness remains for clinical TTE: methods are not standard in EHR phenotyping pipelines; Wang et al. (2026) still promote NLP for eligibility without a required leakage audit; temporal locking plus formal comparison of embedding-versus-structured treatment prediction is recommended in the agenda and only partially operationalized outside medicine. Sensitivity and distillation quantify or reduce leakage; they do not make an embedding's causal role fully interpretable dimension-by-dimension. The problem is therefore partially solved in the text-as-confounder literature and still under-adopted in clinical emulation practice.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Clinical-note and other high-dimensional embeddings used as baseline covariates can encode treatment-related content even when timestamps precede assignment; formal treatment-leakage methods and text distillation exist, but they are not yet standard practice in target trial emulations, and no routine test fully certifies that an embedding encodes only pre-treatment prognosis.

resolving_work.title: Conceptualizing Treatment Leakage in Text-based Causal Inference
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Defines treatment leakage when text used for confounding adjustment also carries treatment signal, including leakage from pre-assignment future-referencing language; establishes the identification and estimation problem the agenda restates.
resolving_work.quote: In this article, we define the treatment-leakage problem, and discuss the identification as well as the estimation challenges it raises.

resolving_work.title: Detecting and Mitigating Treatment Leakage in Text-Based Causal Inference: Distillation and Sensitivity Analysis
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Provides formal statistical definitions of treatment leakage plus automatic and semi-automatic distillers and leakage sensitivity analysis so that text representations can be purged or stress-tested for treatment-predictive content before adjustment.
resolving_work.quote: Despite growing recognition of this issue, no systematic methods exist for identifying and mitigating treatment leakage in text-as-confounder applications. This paper addresses this gap through three contributions.

counter_evidence.quote: If treatment leakage exists, then using the text to adjust for confounding will lead to post-treatment (collider) bias, because the text also contains information about the treatment.

opinions.rationale: Feuerriegel et al. (2024) again bind individualized causal ML to classical identification assumptions; that supports the problem's premise without solving subgroup practice. Tools already recommended in the agenda exist in partial form: honest sample splitting in causal forests (Wager and Athey lineage), propensity trimming and common-support restriction, and various hierarchical or shrinkage approaches to unstable strata. Recent applied causal-forest work still documents poor within-stratum overlap and relies on post hoc trimming (e.g., 2025 Scientific Reports-style pipelines). What remains open is the joint operational problem the statement names: subgroup and protected-group HTE is often the scientific target; those strata systematically have the worst overlap and measurement quality; and there is no adopted standard that reports subgroup-specific data support, calibration, and differential assumption plausibility next to every CATE so that a poorly supported protected-group estimate cannot be read as a finding. Overlap is a data property no estimator repairs. Fairness-aware HTE and group-bias CATE work is active on arXiv and conference tracks but has not certified subgroup effects under differential access and measurement. Status remains open; the caveat is that honesty, trimming, and shrinkage are available components, not a field solution to protected-stratum extrapolation.
